query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy such as NbMoTaW can be used to enhance glass‐forming ability because its high mixing entropy combined with significant atomic size mismatches reduces the driving force for crystallization when rapidly cooled.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous molten NbMoTaW refractory high‐entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Application of rapid cooling methods (e.g., melt spinning) to bypass crystallization kinetics
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere and cooling rates high enough to achieve vitrification, under conditions similar to those used for preparing metallic glasses
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy and atomic size disparity among Nb, Mo, Ta, and W promote disordered atomic arrangements
generation.mechanism: The extensive atomic size differences and high mixing entropy lower the nucleation driving force for crystalline phase formation, thereby favoring the creation of an amorphous structure when solidification occurs under sufficiently rapid cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: An amorphous (glassy) structure of the NbMoTaW alloy with improved glass‐forming ability compared to conventional alloys with lower entropy and size mismatch.
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory alloys or alloys with lower mixing entropy and less atomic size disparity that typically crystallize under comparable cooling rates
generation.boundary: This enhanced glass‐forming ability is expected only for compositions that maintain high mixing entropy and substantial atomic size differences; deviations from the optimal composition or insufficient cooling rates may not yield a fully amorphous structure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical cooling rate necessary for vitrification and the reproducibility of forming a glassy phase in NbMoTaW require further experimental clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the NbMoTaW alloy and subject it to a series of rapid cooling experiments (e.g., melt spinning) at varying cooling rates. Use X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and differential scanning calorimetry to assess whether an amorphous structure forms.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns (absence of sharp crystalline peaks indicates amorphous nature)
Transmission electron microscopy images (to confirm the lack of long-range order)
Differential scanning calorimetry (to detect glass transition behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high cooling rates consistently yield a crystalline or partially crystalline microstructure rather than a fully amorphous glass, it would falsify the hypothesis that NbMoTaW enhances glass‐forming ability via the proposed mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ].
